title: Soft Fallback Sherpa and Tenant Fidelity Mapper - PRD (rough)
body:
Summary:

This rough PRD proposes two complementary features for Dedicated capacity: (1) Sherpa — a small coordinated soft-fallback pool and orchestration pattern that guides tenant traffic through graceful-degradation paths when dedicated pool headroom is exhausted, and (2) Tenant Fidelity Mapper — a lightweight per-tenant scoring and mapping system that converts tenant requirements into fidelity profiles (quantization level, KV cache reuse aggressiveness, batch tolerance, and preferred model variants). Together these aim to reduce hard preemptions, preserve important SLAs, and make burst behavior predictable and auditable.

Context / problem:

We routinely see tenant bursts that temporarily exceed reserved capacity. Current options are: hard throttle (bad UX), immediate failover to hosted variants (data plane hop + security/latency tradeoffs), or ad-hoc backfills. This results in noisy neighbor incidents, unclear cost tradeoffs, and manual operator intervention. Product and SRE ask for: fewer hard preemptions, clear SLA-preserving fallbacks, and automated tenant-specific fidelity decisions to avoid one-size-fits-all throttling.

Goals:
- Reduce hard preemption incidents by enabling controlled, observable fallbacks for transient bursts.
- Preserve tenant SLA priorities (latency-sensitive vs best-effort) via per-tenant fidelity profiles.
- Make burst economics predictable (cost to tenant and to Redwood ops).
- Provide operators tooling to inspect fallback decisions and replay behavior.

Non-goals:
- Not a replacement for long-term capacity commitments and overcommit controls.
- Not addressing on-prem physical node scheduling (that remains in infra roadmap).
- Not full-featured ML-driven autoscaler at launch — this is heuristics + telemetry-first.

Design overview:

High-level pieces:
1) Sherpa pool: a small cross-tenant soft-fallback pool of ephemeral workers (GPU-backed) that accept degraded work under controlled contracts. Sherpa provides: pre-warmed kernels, shorter-lived KV caches, and enforced fidelity caps.

2) Tenant Fidelity Mapper (TFM): a per-tenant declarative mapping (and score) that maps tenant signals to fidelity profiles. Signals include tenant tier, request latency SLO, historical degradation tolerance, and explicit tenant preferences (via console).

3) Fallback Orchestrator: routing policy engine that decides when to route to Sherpa vs. other fallbacks (hosted, throttle). The orchestrator consults TFM, current pool headroom, and a burst budget ledger.

4) Burst Budget Ledger: soft credit accounting per tenant (time-windowed credits). Helps quantify how many requests can route to Sherpa and with what fidelity. Credits decay over time and can be topped by customer config (purchase or reserve credits).

5) Observability / Ops UI: new console views: per-tenant fallback traces, fidelity change timeline, cost delta estimation for routed requests, and a replay tool to re-simulate fallback decisions.

Sherpa behavior and constraints:
- Sherpa accepts only requests labeled by orchestrator with a fidelity profile. Requests routed to Sherpa have metadata headers to ensure downstream billing and auditing.
- Sherpa has hard safety caps: per-tenant concurrency limit, per-model concurrency limit, and an overall capacity cap to avoid Sherpa becoming a sink for noisy tenants.
- Compute on Sherpa is pre-configured for efficient low-fidelity runs: mixed-precision quantization, aggressive KV reuse policies, smaller context windows.
- Sherpa returns a standardized degradation token in the response header (fallback: sherpa, fidelity: low-2) which client SDKs can surface.

Tenant Fidelity Mapper details:
- Inputs: tenant tier, configured latency SLO, recent user-visible quality degradation incidents, recent eval results (if customer supplies), and console overrides.
- Outputs: a simple profile name (e.g., fidelity:high, fidelity:balanced, fidelity:low-2) plus a prioritized list of knobs: target quantization (int8/4), max output length ratio, batching aggressiveness, whether to allow hosted fallback, and whether to allow Sherpa.
- TFM is intentionally simple JSON mapping stored in customer config with a small set of predefined profiles to keep behavior predictable.

Autoscaling & interaction with existing reserved capacity:
- Primary autoscaler remains responsible for long-lived scale-up/down and prewarming. Sherpa is NOT a substitute for real autoscale; Sherpa is a soft buffer.
- The Fallback Orchestrator will only route to Sherpa once autoscaler signals that immediate capacity cannot be provisioned within tenant latency SLO window.
- If bursts are sustained, orchestrator surfaces signals to product autoscaler and optionally triggers an operator alert and a suggested reservation increase for the tenant.

Eviction / fairness policy:
- Burst Budget Ledger enforces per-tenant windows. When Sherpa is saturated, eviction order is based on: tenant SLA tier (priority), remaining burst credits, and recency of fallback.
- Gentle decay: tenants recently pushed to Sherpa will get prioritized reclamation to minimize oscillation.

Billing and economics:
- Requests served by Sherpa are billed with a transparent surcharge (higher per-token cost than reserved pool but lower than on-demand hosted).
- Burst credits can be purchased or included in reserved contracts as optional add-ons.

Observability and tracing:
- Request lifecycle: route decision, reasoning (lack of headroom / preemption risk), fidelity profile used, Sherpa allocation id, cost delta.
- Console: per-tenant timeline with counts of Sherpa-graded requests, cost impact, and quality regression signals (via eval snapshots if available).

Operational runbook (draft):
- When Sherpa utilization > 70%: ops receives slack alert with top 5 tenants by Sherpa volume.
- If Sherpa hit 90% for > 10 minutes: automated mitigation sequence: tighten per-tenant concurrency cap, suspend low-priority tenants, open an incident if majority traffic is priority tenants.
- Post-incident: run the replay tool to identify how mapping decisions could be improved; consider temporary reserve bump offers to affected tenants.

Metrics and success criteria:
- Primary: reduction in hard preemptions/evictions by >30% for pilot tenants in first 90 days.
- Secondary: average customer-visible latency increase for Sherpa-routed requests < 30% of baseline for balanced profile; cost/P95 change tracked.
- Operational: mean time to detect Sherpa saturation < 2 minutes; false positive fallback events < 5% of routed fallbacks.

Rollout plan (phases):
1) Internal pilot: product + SRE traffic only, read-only TFM with manual approvals for routing. (2 weeks)
2) Opt-in customers: provide console toggle + per-tenant budget; run 4 customers with different workloads (chat, summarization, embeddings). (6 weeks)
3) Gradual enablement: tiered enablement for all reserved customers with clear pricing and console controls. (8 weeks)

Open questions / risks:
- Behavioral quality: how to measure subjective regressions automatically? Need integration with eval framework.
- Gaming: tenants might attempt to circumvent fidelity mapping to avoid surcharges. Need audit logs and enforcement.
- Cost allocation accuracy across shared Sherpa pool requires careful tagging of GPU-time.
- Sherpa provisioning sizing is non-trivial; we need an initial pilot size and fast scale-up playbook.

Next actions / immediate engineering asks:
- PoC for TFM store (small JSON mapping service + console UI stub) and a simulator that replays past tenant traffic to estimate Sherpa volume. (infra + console)
- Lightweight Sherpa binary build: runtime flags to enforce small KV caches and quantization presets. (serving-runtime)
- Orchestrator rule engine prototype (policy DSL) and a sandboxed route that can be toggled per-tenant. (platform-engineering)
- Observability: implement fallback headers, persist routing decisions, and a first-cut console trace view. (observability + console)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic and conservative: keep mapping rules small and the Sherpa pool bounded. We want to prove the UX and economics before doing ML-driven autoscale.
- Looking for feedback on: priority ordering for evictions, surcharge pricing band for Sherpa, and how conservative to make the initial fidelity profiles.

References and background threads:
- Internal incident notes: slack thread #dedicated-bursts (see linked Confluence).
- Related PRD ideas: multiple docs in product/dedicated discussing burst credits and graceful fallback; this tries to unify under a named Sherpa pattern.
